sources.note: Nothing on stress; Thakik (= Dagik) mentioned only for dialects/orthography; tone sections (4.0, 5.5) concern Lumun (two tones, low functional load), Asharon (no contrastive tone per Norton 1994) and Tocco.

sources.citation: Quint, Nicolas. 2019. Review of Vanderelst, John: A grammar of Dagik, A Kordofanian language of Sudan. Journal of African Languages and Linguistics 40(2): 311-316. doi:10.1515/jall-2019-0012.
sources.note: Nothing on stress. Reports ch. 2 (pp. 9-36) treats vowels, consonants, syllable structure and 'the tonal system'; tone gets only pp. 35-36 (three mid-tone heights ML/MLL/MLLL); Vanderelst holds 'vowel lengthening is conditioned, not contrastive' (p. 16, section pp. 16-18) and omits length and tone from transcriptions.

sources.citation: Schadeberg, Thilo C. 2018. Review of John Vanderelst, A Grammar of Dagik (Köln: Köppe, 2016). Linguistique et Langues Africaines 4: 133-139. doi:10.4000/lla.10330.
sources.note: Nothing on stress. Reports (p. 134) that Vanderelst's phonology chapter covers vowels, consonants, syllable structure and tone; 'Tone receives just a sketchy documentation and analysis (p. 35f.). The author shows that tone must be lexically contrastive with nouns (p. 41f.) and adjectives (p. 143f.), though not with verbs where tones depend on inflectional categories (p. 85-87). Tone is left unmarked..'; also automatic vowel lengthening in CVːCV vs nasal lengthening in CVNːV.

sources.citation: Smits, Heleen. 2017. A grammar of Lumun: a Kordofanian language of Sudan. Utrecht: LOT (Leiden PhD).
sources.note: Describes Lumun, not Dagik; Dagik cited only for a tap/trill contrast (Vanderelst p.c.), vowel system and pronouns. No statement on Dagik prosody.

sources.citation: Norton, Russell & Thomas Kuku Alaki. 2015. The Talodi languages: a comparative-historical analysis. Occasional Papers in the Study of Sudanese Languages 11: 47-161 (whole OPSL 11 volume downloaded from the Internet Archive copy of sil.org).

sources.note: Nothing on stress. Sec. 3.2.5 'Note on Length and Tone' (p. 107): 'We omit analysis of prosodic features for lack of data and for lack of functional load'; vowel length non-contrastive across Talodi (long vowels in non-final position / monosyllables); 'Sources repeatedly show two tone levels in Talodi languages (.. Vanderelst 2015), but tone is often contextually determined and minimal pairs are rare'.
